analytic.title: DNA from owl pellet bones uncovers hidden biodiversity

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Owl pellets are a useful tool for inventorying small mammals and a robust complement to traditional trapping methods.

Here we assessed if bone samples recovered from Barn owl pellets in the Neotropics represent a viable source of modern DNA. We used the upper incisor of rodents and jaws of marsupials of pellet material for DNA extraction and amplification. Extraction and amplification success depended on the type of bone element used, being much higher from rodent incisors. The amplification success of small (429 bp) and large (801 bp) mitochondrial cytochrome b fragments was relatively similar, suggesting that DNA was not severely degraded, probably because our pellet samples were less than 8 years old. Eleven species of small mammals were identified, from which two are new to the study area: Gracilinanus emiliae and Marmosops pinheiroi. These records represent the southeastern boundary of both species, and extended their geographic distribution 370 km (G. emiliae) and 700 km (M. pinheiroi) to the south. Moreover, two of three detected species of Oecomys occurring in sympatry may represent undescribed species. The use of molecular analysis as a complement to morphological analysis of pellet bones is very effective in species identification, especially considering poorly known and elusive species, such as those reported here. The search for owl pellets during fieldwork should be a common practice among mammalogists in the Neotropics because this material provides a valuable non-invasive source of DNA, often revealing previously undetected species and sometimes uncovering new species.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The Neotropical region hosts one of the richest mammalian fauna of the world (see Patterson & Costa, 2012), and is considered a 'natural museum' where new genera and species discoveries have grown at a fast pace over recent years (e.g., Guti errez, Jansa, & Voss, 2010;Pardiñas, Lessa, Teta, Salazar-Bravo, & Câmara, 2014;Percequillo, Weksler, & Costa, 2011;Voss, Lim, Diaz-Nieto, & Jansa, 2013). These new taxa largely consist of small mammals: bats, marsupials and rodents weighing less than 1 kg. Despite these advances, our knowledge on several species is still very scarce, and based on scattered specimens from a few collecting localities (e.g., Brandão, da Rocha, Dantas, & Pascoal, 2014;Rocha, Fonseca, Zhou, Leite, & Costa, 2012;Voss, Fleck, & Jansa, 2009;Voss et al., 2013). This collecting gap prevents a full understanding of Neotropical diversity and its associated historical phylogeographic patterns (Patton, da Silva, & Malcolm, 2000). Some studies evaluated field techniques and suggested methods to improve the effectiveness of Neotropical small mammal surveys (e.g., C aceres, N apoli, & Hannibal, 2011;Lambert, Malcolm, & Zimmerman, 2005;Ribeiro-J unior, Rossi, Miranda, & Avila-Pires, 2011;Voss & Emmons, 1996), because several species either avoid trapping devices or fail to be detected due to their elusive behaviour and/or low densities. Owl pellets are a useful tool for inventorying small mammals and a robust complement to traditional trapping methods (e.g., Bonvicino & Bezerra, 2003;Rocha, Ferreira, Leite, Fonseca, & Costa, 2011a;Souza, Asfora, Lira, & Ast ua, 2010;Teta, Gonz alez-Fischer, Codesido, & Bilenca, 2010;Torre, Arrizabalaga, & Flaquer, 2004). Barn owls (Tyto alba), for example, are specialized predators that feed mainly on small mammals, and prey bone remains are regurgitated in the form of pellets (Bellocq, 2000). Given that the Barn owl is a cosmopolitan species (Sick, 1997), these pellets are often available in several different habitats, thus representing a low-cost, effective tool in detecting small mammals.

Previous studies have already confirmed the potential of pellet bones as a modern DNA source in temperate areas (Bu s et al., 2014;Poulakakis, Lymberakis, Paragamian, & Mylonas, 2005;Taberlet & Fumagalli, 1996). However, non-invasive samples in tropical regions are easily degraded due to climatic conditions (e.g., Mukherjee, Ashalakshmi, Home, & Ramakrishnan, 2010;Vynne, Baker, Breuer, & Wasse, 2012). Furthermore, the accelerated DNA degradation of ancient bones has also been related to the exposure to high humidity and temperatures, typical of the tropical climate (Singh, Joglekar, & Koziol, 2011;Smith, Chamberlain, Riley, Stringer, & Collins, 2003). Therefore, we aim to assess if bone samples recovered from Barn owl pellets in the Neotropics represent a viable source of modern DNA, and if this genetic material uncovers species that have not been detected by other methods.

div.head: General strategy
div.p: Herein we followed a strategy similar to that described by Taberlet and Fumagalli (1996). We extracted DNA from bones found in Barn owl pellets to assess if enough DNA could be obtained from this material to proceed with downstream analyses. Amplified DNA allowed us to identify consumed prey and to check whether possible contamination could have occurred with DNA from the predator or from other prey within each pellet. The mitochondrial (mtDNA) cytochrome b (cytb) gene was chosen for the analyses because this marker has been commonly used to distinguish sister species of mammals (e.g., Agrizzi et al., 2012;Bradley & Baker, 2001), and also because there is a very large database of cytb sequences available from published sources for comparison (e.g., Patton et al., 2000;Rocha et al., 2011b;Voss et al., 2013). Finally, we also tested if we could amplify mtDNA fragments of several sizes using different pairs of primers, thus allowing us to assess the level of DNA degradation in this material. The obtained sequences were then used in phylogenetic analyses to place the samples into a taxonomic context.

div.head: Biological samples
div.p: Barn owl pellets were collected in two different areas of the mid-Araguaia River in central Brazil in 2007and 2008(see Rocha et al., 2011a for detailed information on collected material and sampled habitats). Small mammal samples were screened and identified to the lowest taxonomic level possible (Rocha et al., 2011a). After this procedure, bony elements were stored in a dry place without any chemical preservative. All samples have been deposited in the mammal collection of the Universidade Federal do Esp ırito Santo (UFES), Vit oria, Brazil.

For the purposes of this study, bony elements were chosen at random for each studied species and also for unidentified material (Table 1). For rodents, the upper incisor was removed, and for marsupials, the entire jaw was used. Due to the taxonomic value of marsupial jaws, and considering the destruction of this material during DNA extraction, we first documented this material by taking photographs and two measurements: mandible length (MAD) and length of the lower molar series (LM1À4).

div.head: DNA extraction, amplification and sequencing
div.p: DNA extraction and PCR preparation procedures were performed in physically isolated facilities. The clean DNA room is exclusively used for DNA extraction from museum skins and bones, and is equipped with a UVchamber, which was regularly turned on between each procedure. Protective lab coat, disposable facemask, lab cap and gloves were used to avoid contamination.

We also followed Poulakakis et al.'s (2005) protocol to prevent possible contamination. Bones were always handled with gloves and forceps, and were submitted to a three-step wash in the clean DNA room. Bone outer surfaces were washed in sterile distilled water and allowed to dry. This first step was followed by a 10% bleach wash to remove previous contamination, and by another sterile distilled water wash to remove excess bleach, which could affect down-stream steps.

Before DNA extraction, bones were wrapped in a UV-sterilized aluminium foil and placed in a mortar. Liquid nitrogen was poured over the packet and the sample was carefully ground to a powder. The resulting bony powder and fragments were placed in 1.5 mL microtubes for further procedures. DNA was extracted from bony powder and fragments using the DNeasy Blood & Tissue Qiagen kit following manufacturer indications, but with some modifications. Columns of the QiaQuick PCR purification Qiagen kit were used instead of the DNeasy kit, allowing better collection of small fragments (Rowe et al., 2011). Final elution was conducted in two steps, in which 100 mL of AE buffer was added twice to the columns, generating two batches. AE buffer was diluted in a proportion of 1:10 with sterile water, and warmed at 70 C. The first elution step lasted for 30 min and the second lasted for 15 min (P. B. Chaves & S. L oss, pers. comm.). To assess cross-contamination during extraction and amplification, a negative control (1.5 mL microtube without bone powder) was treated identically through both procedures. To check DNA quality, 4 mL of each sample was run on a 2% agarose gel. DNA in the final elution solution was concentrated using a heater at 55 C, because no fragment was seen in the gel in most samples.

PCR amplifications were performed for two fragment sizes of the mitochondrial cytochrome b (cytb) gene. First, small cytb fragments (429 bp) were amplified by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) using the primers MVZ05 and MVZ04 (Smith & Patton, 1993), and then larger fragments (801 bp) were amplified using the primers MVZ05 and MVZ16 (Smith & Patton, 1993). PCR reactions were performed in a 25 mL total volume, including 2.5 mL of 10 £ PCR buffer, 1.0 mL of MgCl 2 (50 mM), 1.0 mL of BSA (10mg/mL), 0.5 mL of deoxyribonucleotide triphosphate (dNTP) mixture (10 mM), 0.25 mL of Platinum Ò Taq DNA polymerase (Invitrogen Life Technologies), and 0.3 mL of each primer (10 mM). Due to differences in DNA concentration and to the potential presence of inhibitors that could prevent amplification, we did not normalize the amount of DNA in each PCR reaction. First, we used 2 mL of the extract in each PCR reaction. For samples that failed to amplify or presented a very light band, we gradually increased the amount of DNA in the PCR reaction until a strong band was obtained. If no amplification was detected after several PCR attempts, we diluted the samples to check for the presence of inhibitors (Bu s et al., 2014). Amplifications were performed using the following PCR profile: initial denaturation at 94 C for 5 min, followed by 39 cycles with denaturation at 94 C for 30 s, annealing at 48 C for 45 s, polymerization at 72 C for 45 s, and a final extension at 72 C for 5 min. PCR products were visualized by electrophoresis on 2% agarose gels.

div.head: Phylogenetic analyses
div.p: Sequence alignment was performed using CLUSTALW algorithm implemented in MEGA 6 (Tamura et al., 2013), with posterior manual edition. We performed BLAST searches in GenBank (http://blast.st-va.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/ Blast.cgi) in order to determine the approximate association of the obtained sequences with published records. All sequences generated in this study have been deposited in GenBank (Table 1). Pairwise sequence divergences were obtained in MEGA, using the Kimura2-parameter model (Kimura, 1980) for comparisons with those available in the literature. They are reported here as average § standard error calculated using 500 bootstrap replicates in MEGA. Phylogenetic relationships of Thylamyini marsupials and Oecomys rodents were estimated through Bayesian inference (BI) in MrBayes 3.1.2 (Ronquist & Huelsenbeck, 2003). The model of nucleotide substitution was selected using MrModeltest (Nylander, 2004). Trees were sampled every 100 of 10 7 generations until Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) became stationary, i.e., when standard deviation of split frequencies was below 0.01 (Ronquist, van der Mark, & Huelsenbeck, 2009). MCMC convergence was also checked in Tracer v. 1.6 (Rambaut & Drummond, 2013), where we confirmed if effective sample sizes (ESS) were above 200. A 50% majority rule consensus tree was obtained after 'burn-in' of 25% of the sample points to generate Bayesian posterior probabilities (BPP). Consensus trees were visualized in FigTree 1.4 (http://tree.bio.ed.ac. uk/software/figtree/).

div.head: Extraction and amplification success
div.p: Extraction and amplification success depended on the type of bone element used (Table 1). Band intensity in agarose gels varied among PCR products, especially among samples of marsupial jaws and rodent incisors (Fig. 1), and subsequently affected sequencing success. We were able to obtain viable sequences from only five out of 11 marsupial jaw samples (45.45%), while 19 out of 22 rodent incisor samples yielded viable sequences (86.36%).

The amplification success of small (429 bp) and large (801 bp) cytb fragments was relatively similar: 69.7% (23 viable sequences) in the former and 57.6% (19 viable sequences) in the latter (Table 1). From the 10 samples that did not result in viable sequences, only two (FSF118m and FSF144r) presented contamination with human DNA, and no other contamination was detected (among consumed prey and/or predator).

div.head: Molecular identification and phylogenetic analyses
div.p: We identified 11 species of small mammals, from which two are new to the study area: Gracilinanus emiliae and Marmosops pinheiroi. All, but one (FSF149r), molecular Fig. 1. Agarose gel (2%) of eight DNA amplifications using samples from marsupial jaws and rodent incisors obtained for barn owl pellets. From the left: lane 1: molecular-weight marker (100 bp ladder); lanes 2À5: PCR products of two marsupial and two rodent samples using the primers MVZ05 and MVZ04; lanes 7À10: PCR products of two marsupial and two rodent samples using the primers MVZ05 and MVZ16; lanes 6 and 11: negative controls (i.e., no DNA template).

identifications matched previous morphological identifications (Table 1). The sample FSF149r had been previously identified as Euryoryzomys sp., and has now been identified as Hylaeamys megacephalus based on the cytb sequence (Table 1). Seven out of 14 previously unidentified samples have now been identified using molecular data, four of them only to the genus level, or species group (Cryptonanus sp., Oecomys gr. roberti and Oecomys gr. bicolor, see below).

Phylogenetic analyses using partial cytb sequences recovered from marsupial jaws allowed the identification of three species of small marsupials of the group Thylamyini (Fig. 2). Samples FSF60m, FSF77m and FSF92m formed a highly supported (BPP D 1.0) cluster with a sample of G. emiliae from Peru. Although intraspecific genetic distance between these samples is relatively high (5.4 § 1.0%), interspecific genetic distance between this cluster and the closest-related species of Gracilinanus is even higher, ranging from 14.3 § 1.8% (G. aceramarcae) to 18.2 § 1.8% (G. agilis). The sample FSF133m formed a highly supported cluster (BPP D 1.0) with samples of M. pinheiroi from Brazil (Bel em, Par a), French Guiana, Guyana and Surinam. More specifically, FSF133m is part of a clade of M. pinheiroi from the south of the Amazon River (SAM, Fig. 2), and the genetic distance between SAM and the northern clade (NAM) is relatively high (6.1 § 0.8%). Interspecific genetic distance to closely related species of Marmosops ranges from 14.5 § 1.6% (M. pakaraimae) to16.9 § 1.8% (M. parvidens). One marsupial sample (FSF3m) grouped with C. chacoensis, but with no support (BPP < 0.95). When compared with the four extant species of Cryptonanus, FSF3m presented lower genetic distance to C. chacoensis (4.6 § 0.9%), than to C. agricolai (7.3 § 1.1%), C. unduaviensis (11.8 § 1.5%) and C. guahybae (12.1 § 1.4%).

Phylogenetic analyses using partial cytb sequences recovered from rodent incisors allowed the identification of three species of Oecomys (Fig. 3). Four samples were recovered as part of two well-supported clades: FSF107r and FSF140r within Oecomys roberti; and FSF53r and FSF68r within Oecomys gr. roberti. These two clades show high genetic distance between them (6.5 § 0.9%). One sample (FSF34r) is part of the O. biolor C O. cleberi clade, but did not group with either. This sample showed high genetic distance to the closest related species O. bicolor (6.1 § 0.9%) and O. cleberi (5.7 § 0.8%), and even higher genetic distance to O. roberti (9.0 § 1.0%) and Oecomys gr. roberti (7.5 § 1.1%) that occur in the same geographic area.

div.head: Discussion
div.p: The use of owl pellets in small mammal surveys is growing in the Neotropics (e.g., Baglan & Catzeflis, 2014;Rocha et al., 2011a;Souza et al., 2010;Teta et al., 2010), and this potential source of modern DNA must be evaluated. We were able to amplify large mtDNA fragments, suggesting that DNA was not severely degraded, probably because our samples were less than eight years old. The age of pellet remains has an impact on the level of PCR inhibition, which is higher in samples older than twelve years (Bu s et al., 2014). Cross-contamination among the different prey consumed did not occur in our study, but contamination with human DNA was recorded in two samples. Although prey DNA is protected against degradation and contamination inside the bones (Taberlet & Fumagalli, 1996), the outer surface is more vulnerable to contamination. We suggest increasing the time and concentration of the bleach wash step to remove previous contaminants. For example, Bu s et al. ( 2014) soaked samples in 15% bleach for 10 minutes, which could be a reasonable improvement of the protocol used here.

The DNA extraction and amplification success rates obtained here corroborate previous studies conducted using specimens from temperate regions (e.g. Bu s et al., 2014;Poulakakis et al., 2005;Taberlet & Fumagalli, 1996). Although DNA from non-invasive samples collected in the Neotropical region are easily degraded due to climatic conditions (e.g., Mukherjee et al., 2010;Vynne et al., 2012), our amplification success rate of mtDNA from rodent incisors was similar to that reported from temperate areas in eastern Europe (Bu s et al., 2014). The amplification success rate was much higher from rodent incisors (86.36%) than marsupial jaws (45.45%) because DNA is better preserved in teeth than in jaws (Bu s et al., 2014). Indeed, studies using ancient samples often use teeth as a source of DNA (e.g., Chan, Lacey, Pearson, & Hadly, 2005;Hadly, Tuinen, Chan, & Heiman, 2003;Hofreiter, Serre, Poinar, Kuch, & P€ a€ abo, 2001;Spaeth, Tuinen, Chan, Terca, & Hadly, 2009). Despite a relatively low amplification success, our results with marsupial jaws suggest that this material is very important, especially considering that marsupial jaws usually remain unidentified using morphological characters only (Rocha et al., 2011a).

Previous studies in the same Amazonia-Cerrado ecotone detected a total of 24 species of small mammals (see Bezerra, Carmignotto, &Rodrigues, 2009 andRocha et al., 2011b for species lists). Here we added two species, Gracilinanus emiliae and Marmosops pinheiroi, both previously known mainly from northern Amazonia (Brandão et al., 2014;Voss et al., 2009;2013). These records represent the southeastern boundary of both species, and extended their geographic distribution 370 km (G. emiliae) and 700 km (M. pinheiroi) to the south (Fig. 4).

Barn owl pellets have been suggested as a complementary tool in inventorying small mammals (e.g. Bonvicino & Bezerra, 2003;Scheibler & Christoff, 2007;Souza et al., 2010). Previous authors have already extended the geographic distribution of marsupials (Souza et al., 2010) and even detected an undescribed species of Akodon for the first time using owl pellets (Pardiñas, D'Ell ıa, Cirignoli, & Suarez, 2005). The use of molecular analysis as a complement to morphological analysis of pellet bones is very effective in species identification, especially considering poorly known and elusive species, such as those reported here.

Thylamyini marsupials and rodents of the genus Oecomys are both diverse and poorly known groups in terms of taxonomy (e.g., Patton et al., 2000;Rocha et al., 2012;Voss & Jansa, 2009;Voss, Lunde, & Jansa, 2005;Voss et al., 2009). Our phylogenetic analysis of DNA sequences from owl pellet bones revealed three sympatric species of Thylamyini occurring in the AmazoniaÀCerrado ecotone. Four samples were assigned to either G. emiliae or M. pinheiroi, in spite of relatively high intraspecific genetic distances recorded. Voss et al. (2013) have already reported this intraspecific divergence in two clades of M. pinheiroi separated by the Amazon River, showing that the genetic structure of this species was shaped by the river. The high intraspecific genetic distance of G. emiliae can be explained by the 2500 km separating our collecting locality and the closest specimen with cytb sequence available, which is from Peru (Voss et al., 2005).

Specimens of Cryptonanus from central Brazil in the Amazonia-Cerrado ecotone and southwestern Cerrado have been commonly assigned to C. agricolai (e.g. Bezerra et al., 2009;Faria, Nascimento, de Oliveira, & Bonvicino, 2013). Our specimen, however, is closer to C. chacoensis from Paraguay (specimen identified by Robert Voss, Teta, D'Elia, Flores, & de la Sancha, 2009) than to C. agricolai and only a taxonomic revision of this genus will help clarify the taxonomic status of the specimen reported here.

Our phylogenetic analyses revealed three species of Oecomys occurring in sympatry in the Amazonia-Cerrado ecotone, and two of them may represent undescribed spe-Medium-sized specimens of the genus Oecomys previously reported from this area were designated as Oecomys sp. due to the high genetic distance to O. roberti, the sister species that also occurs in the same area (Rocha et al., 2011b). Here we refer to these samples as Oecomys gr. roberti until further taxonomic data are available (Rocha et al., in prep). A small-sized Oecomys was also detected in this area by Bezerra et al. (2009), and identified as O. bicolor due to its small size and other morphological features that characterize this species (Bezerra et al., 2009;Patton et al., 2000). One of the samples that we analysed (FSF 34r) is close to O. bicolor and O. cleberi, but shows relatively high divergence from both (5.7À6.1%), and we refer it to as Oecomys gr. bicolor. Rocha et al. (2012) have already suggested that O. bicolor is probably restricted to Amazonia, thus we believe that this small-sized species of Oecomys from the Amazonia-Cerrado ecotone represents an undescribed species of the O. bicolor group, reinforcing the need of a full taxonomic revision of this genus.

The Neotropical small mammal fauna is still poorly known in terms of basic knowledge regarding taxonomy, ecology and evolution (Patton et al., 2000). Intensive fieldwork is still needed to furnish scientific collections with voucher specimens, which are the foundation for taxonomic studies. The search for owl pellets during fieldwork should be a common practice among mammalogists in the Neotropics because this material typically provides a large number of small mammal skulls that can be preserved as museum specimens and a non-invasive source of DNA (Taberlet & Fumagalli, 1996), often revealing previously undetected species and sometimes uncovering new species. Moreover, considering that small mammals are hosts and vectors of several human pathogens (e.g., Oliveira et al., 2014), searching for owl pellets as a source of DNA would represent a less hazardous method for field mammalogists.
